extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent applicants, Patent Office officials, and appellate judges (U.S. patent appeals)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules applied in appeals from the U.S. Commissioner of Patents concerning patentability, priority of invention, admissibility and weight of evidence, and the limited scope of judicial review under the 1839 Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of judicial review on appeal (§11 act of March 3, 1839)
rubrics_metrics.description: The revision by the judge is to be confined to the grounds of the Commissioner's decision, fully set forth in writing, touching all the points involved by the reasons of appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The judge may consider only the points raised in the appellant's reasons and the grounds the Commissioner set forth; all original papers and evidence are to be laid before the judge and returned with the opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's duty to set forth grounds in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner is required by the 11th section of the act of March 3, 1839 to fully set forth in writing the grounds of his decision touching the points involved in the reasons of appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The written grounds define the scope of what the court may review on appeal; omission or vagueness can constrain review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for taking and considering evidence (Commissioner's 4th rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: "That no evidence, statement or declaration, touching the matter at issue, shall be considered upon the said day of hearing, which shall not have been taken and filed in compliance with the rule: provided, that if either party shall be unable, from good and sufficient reason, to procure the testimony of a witness or witnesses within the above stipulated time, then it shall be the duty of said party to give notice of the same to the Commissioner of Patents... which last mentioned notice to the Commissioner shall be received by him ten days previous to the day of hearing aforesaid."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibits considering evidence at the hearing unless taken and filed in compliance; contains a proviso for inability to procure testimony requiring ten days' notice. The rule forbids considering such informally-transmitted deposition as evidence on the day of hearing, but does not prevent the Commissioner from looking into it or from postponing the hearing to permit cure of irregularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's discretion to postpone hearings to further justice
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing in the Patent Office laws or rules adopted by the Commissioner to prevent him from postponing the hearing of a cause if, in his opinion, the justice of the case should require it, especially for correcting an irregularity in matters of form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commissioner may postpone hearings to enable parties to cure informality in transmission of evidence or to give both parties opportunity to procure further testimony; denying him that power would 'stifle justice in her own forms.' The proviso in the 4th rule does not dictate what the Commissioner must do on receiving notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections to procedure or evidence must be made at hearing (waiver rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: An objection that did not arise at the time of trial and was not then made should have been raised at trial; failure to object at trial can be a sufficient answer to the later objection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural complaints (e.g., insufficient time to be present at a deposition) are waived if not interposed at the hearing; parties should make timely objections at the proceeding itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness of notice for taking depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Service of notice eleven days before depositions (even when witness and party are separated by long distance) was held to be reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What constitutes 'sufficient time' is evaluated in context (11 days to travel 400 miles was reasonable in the cited case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility rules — letters, hearsay and competence of particular statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain documentary statements (e.g., a letter of Captain Bunker) and declarations relating to dates or internal recollections may be inadmissible or 'not competent evidence' in the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimonial statements about what someone else said as to the exact date, or letters not shown to meet evidentiary prerequisites, will be excluded; each contested item must be evaluated for competency and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposit entries or testimony taken in presence of interested parties may be problematic
rubrics_metrics.description: Depositions taken in the presence of an interested party can raise admissibility or credibility issues (example: a deposition taken in presence of Mr. Cochrane).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of interested parties at the taking of testimony may affect the weight or admissibility; such circumstances should be noted and rebutted if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competency objections can be waived by agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may agree that certain testimony will be heard and considered (e.g., testimony taken before named commissioners up to a certain date), thereby waiving objections to competency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A written agreement by counsel to receive specified testimony operates as a waiver of prior competency objections; competency may still affect credit but not admissibility if waived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability principle — substitution of known mechanical equivalent is not invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The substitution of a known mechanical equivalent (e.g., substituting a pinion for a band) is not an invention within the meaning of the patent law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying a well-known mechanical power or equivalent to a machine, even if it improves the machine, does not necessarily justify a patent claim if it is merely an ordinary power applied to an ordinary purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of combinations — new combination producing a new useful effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentable improvement may consist only of a new combination of known mechanical principles or powers when that particular combination produces a new and useful effect in the manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neither the whole machine nor any single old part is patentable; the novelty must lie in the particular combination that yields a new useful result (example: combining calender rollers, an elastic apron, and a stretching frame to produce corrugated rubber goods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of invention — first inventor requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant must establish that he was the first inventor of the claimed improvement; priority is decided by the evidence as to dates and acts of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence must carry the date of invention prior to the rival claim; testimony, depositions, and contemporaneous acts (reduction to practice, models, use) are evaluated to determine priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice — evidence required to prove it
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that an invention was reduced to practice (in actual operation) is material to establishing priority; absence of such evidence can be fatal to a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters or other documents must meet admissibility standards to count; merely asserting reduction to practice without competent evidence is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie inference from fabricating the machine
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that a person made the machine which contains the claimed combination is prima facie evidence that he was the first inventor of that combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inference can be rebutted by evidence showing the fabricator was working as an employee for another who conceived the invention, by delay in asserting inventorship, by lack of claim, or by other circumstances indicating the fabricator was following directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption regarding employee-made machines (work for hire inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person fabricates a machine while working in his trade for wages and for the benefit of another, there is a presumption the machine was made according to the employer's directions and for the employer's benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burden of proof shifts to the fabricator (claimant) to show the machine was his independent invention rather than work done under the employer's direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay in asserting invention or applying for patent undermines inventorship claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Significant delay in claiming to be the inventor or in applying for patent rights (especially after another obtained a patent) rebuts the inference of inventorship from fabrication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay of many months or years, or waiting until an agreement to indemnify costs, can be used to rebut a claimant's priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegations of surreptitious procurement or misconduct require supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Charges that a patent was obtained surreptitiously or that evidence was suppressed must be supported by competent evidence; absent such proof, the allegations are disregarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court will not accept speculative or unsupported accusations of wrongdoing; specific competent proof is required to sustain such claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge and Commissioner are confined to the evidence of record
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the Commissioner and the reviewing judge can act only on the evidence before them; claims that additional evidence exists but was not produced are the claimant's responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional evidence exists and was not offered, the claimant may pursue other remedies (e.g., a bill in equity under statutory provisions) but cannot prevail on unproduced evidence in the appeal record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight and credibility — interest and surrounding circumstances affect credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where witnesses are competent, their interest and circumstances bearing on testimony affect their credibility; the court weighs testimony in light of such factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witnesses with an interest in the outcome or other potential biases may be admissible but their testimony will be given less weight; agreements may waive competency but not credibility concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dates and recollections — caution about testimony fixing exact dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony recounting another person's statement about a precise date (e.g., 'he said it was on the 7th of February') is not competent evidence to fix the date of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court distinguishes between a witness's own recollection of events and hearsay about what another person said; only competent evidence can establish priority dates.
